newsitem.title: USA: Dow industrials defy gravity, end just shy of 5900.
newsitem.headline: Dow industrials defy gravity, end just shy of 5900.

text.p: After storming past 5800 for the first time on Friday, the Dow industrials flirted with the 5900 barrier Monday as investors continued to heed the siren call of U.S. stocks.

"It's pretty amazing. It's got 6000 written all over it. It's more follow-through (buying) than anything else. Numbers are coming in perfect and there's the belief the Fed won't raise rates," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.
The Dow climbed 51 to about 5889, its second consecutive record closing high, after hitting 5905.47 earlier in the day.

The blue chip index soared 178.66 points last week -- its second biggest weekly point gain ever. Recent economic data point to moderating U.S. growth and benign inflation, raising hopes that the Fed will not raise short-term interest rates at its next policy meeting on September 24.
The S&P 500 surged three to about 684, topping Friday's record closing high of 680.54. The NYSE Composite rose two to about 365, surpassing its previous record closing high of 363.74 set on May 24.
The Nasdaq Composite rose a modest five to about 1194, still off June 5's all-time high finish of 1249.15.

Winners beat losers 13-9 on heavy NYSE trading of about 427 million shares. Stocks got a boost after news Dean Witter raised its stock allocation in its basic asset portfolio to 60 percent from 55, cut cash to 20 percent from 25 and left bonds unchanged at 20 percent. The move reverted its allocation recommendation back to levels suggested earlier this month.

"It seems increasingly clear the Fed won't do anything. That means earnings are not at risk of a hike in interest rates and opens up a window of opportunity for stocks until the election. We're heading past 6000," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.
Some on Wall Street were mystified by the stock boom, noting fundmentals like a long bond near seven percent and moderating corporate earnings growth remain worrisome.

"People's perception has changed more than reality. The market is getting ahead of itself and is getting set for another round like July," BT Brokerage's Benning said, referring to the summer correction.

Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers, agreed, "The fundamentals haven't changed much. The markets assume Clinton will be re-elected and there is the record of poor markets for the first year of second-term presidents."
The company warned of an earnings shortfall for the third quarter and Merrill Lynch downgraded the stock.

Anadigics, which also warned third-quarter results would fall short of Street expectations, lost 7-5/8 to 21-7/8. Goldman Sachs pulled the stock from its recommended list, downgrading Anadigics to market outperform.
Citizens Bancorp rallied 14-3/4 to 47 and Crestar Financial lost 2-1/4 to 59-1/8 after agreeing to merge in a deal estimated at $774 million. Goldman cut Crestar to hold from buy.
Checkfree Corp added 3-3/16 to 21-1/4.

Intuit Inc and CheckFree agreed to a deal in which Intuit will swap Intuit Services Corp, its back-end bill payment processing unit, in exchange for a stake of about 23 percent in CheckFree. Intuit rose 2-1/8 to 32-1/4.
Nike class B shares added 2-3/8 to 121-5/8 after reporting a 24 percent jump in first-quarter profits. Its board approved a two-for-one stock split.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 5.29 to 1193.96.
The S&P 500 index rose 3.44 to 683.98, a record.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk, 212 859 1721
